UNDERSTANDING RESPONSE AND COORDINATION IN PLANTS
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what understanding response and coordination in plants means in plain words.
• Give one clear example linked to Response and Coordination in Plants.
• Correct one common mistake about this page.

INTRODUCTION
----
Understanding Response and Coordination in Plants. Get clear on response and coordination in plants before moving on. How would you explain response and coordination in plants to a classmate in one minute? Use this anchor: Explain Stimuli and plant responses within Response and Coordination in Plants using correct terms and a clear example or calculation. Check every example on this page against that anchor.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Plants respond to stimuli (light, gravity, water, touch) and coordinate growth using plant hormones — they do not have animal-style nerves.
• Tropisms are directional growth responses: the direction of growth depends on the direction of the stimulus (positive = towards, negative = away).
• Key tropisms: phototropism (light), geotropism/gravitropism (gravity), hydrotropism (water), thigmotropism (touch, e.g. climbing tendrils).
• Nastic responses are non-directional: the movement pattern does not depend on stimulus direction (e.g. some flowers opening/closing).
• Auxin redistributed unevenly causes uneven elongation — that is how many tropic bends happen in shoots.
• Exam method: name stimulus → name organ → say positive/negative → give one clear example → reject one mix-up (tropism vs nastic).

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Worked example — phototropism in a shoot:

1. Observation: A potted seedling is lit from the left only. After two days the shoot tip bends left towards the lamp.
2. Stimulus: unidirectional light.
3. Response type: positive phototropism (directional growth towards light).
4. Mechanism (exam level): auxin becomes uneven; the shaded side elongates more, so the shoot curves towards the light.
5. Wrong idea to reject: “The plant walked towards the light” or “This is a nastic response” — the bend direction depends on light direction, so it is a tropism.
6. Conclusion: Shoots show positive phototropism, which helps leaves gain light for photosynthesis.[DIAGRAM]

GEOTROPISM
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what geotropism means in plain words.
• Give one clear example linked to Response and Coordination in Plants.
• Correct one common mistake about this page.

INTRODUCTION
----
Geotropism. Focus on geotropism. Learners often mix up geotropism with a nearby idea. Keep this accurate line instead: Explain Geotropism within Response and Coordination in Plants using correct terms and a clear example or calculation. The worked example proves the difference.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Geotropism (gravitropism) is a directional growth response to gravity.
• Roots are usually positively geotropic (grow downwards); shoots are usually negatively geotropic (grow upwards).
• This helps roots reach water/minerals and shoots reach light.
• If a seedling is laid on its side, the root curves down and the shoot curves up — that is geotropism.
• Distinguish geotropism from hydrotropism (response to water) — they can act together in soil but are different stimuli.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Worked example — geotropism in root and shoot:

1. Observation: A germinating seed is placed on its side. The radicle (young root) curves down; the plumule (young shoot) curves up.
2. Stimulus: gravity.
3. Response: root — positive geotropism; shoot — negative geotropism.
4. Why it matters: roots reach water/minerals; shoots reach light and air.
5. Wrong idea to reject: calling both organs “positively geotropic” — shoots grow against gravity.
6. Conclusion: Geotropism is a directional growth response to gravity with opposite signs in root and shoot.[DIAGRAM]

3. EXAM (4 marks): Define tropism (1), name two tropisms (1), give one example with direction (1), state one difference from nastic responses (1).


ANSWERS
----
1. Auxin becomes higher on the shaded side; that side elongates more; the shoot bends towards the light (positive phototropism).
2. Roots: usually positive geotropism (down). Shoots: usually negative geotropism (up).
3. Tropism = directional growth response. Two of: photo/geo/hydro/thigmo. Example with +/−. Difference: nastic responses are not directional with respect to the stimulus.
